conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. You were admitted last night with a fever. Can you tell me how you've been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. Yeah, I had a fever of 101.2 at home. I felt fine the day before—was even doing chores. But overnight, I had bad night sweats and woke up just feeling 'off.' No chills, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And since then, any nausea, vomiting, or belly pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, none of that. My stools are always loose, but nothing worse than usual. I do have some phlegm I keep clearing, but no cough or sore throat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We ran some tests in the ER. Your blood work showed mild liver enzyme elevations—AST and ALT—but your bilirubin is normal, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that related to my cancer or the stent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but since bilirubin is normal, it doesn’t look like a blockage. We’re concerned about infection, especially with your history, so we started antibiotics just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember getting an IV in the ER. Was it for antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, ceftriaxone and metronidazole. We’ve switched to cefepime and flagyl now for broader coverage while we wait for blood cultures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be on them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see. If we don’t find an infection and you stay fever-free, we may stop them in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I don’t want to be on antibiotics longer than needed, especially with my history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’re also watching your white blood cell count. It was 6.0 in the ER, but this morning it dropped to 2.7.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s low, right? From chemo?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s low, and likely due to your recent gemcitabine/cisplatin. We’ll keep monitoring it. Platelets are also a bit low at 83, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had that before. My oncologist adjusts the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Now, we did a chest X-ray and ultrasound of your abdomen. The chest X-ray showed no pneumonia—just some old scarring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that granuloma for years. Nothing new?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing new. The ultrasound showed your bile ducts are still dilated, like before, but no change. The stent looks in place, and gallbladder has sludge, which we’ve seen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no sign of stent blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. And since your bilirubin is normal, we don’t think so. That’s why we’re leaning away from cholangitis this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Last time I was in for fever, they thought it was the stent, but it got better on its own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I saw that. And this time, no rigors or abdominal pain, which also makes infection less likely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just hope it’s not another bacteremia like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching closely. Blood cultures are drawn, and if they stay negative and you stay fever-free, we’ll be confident there’s no bloodstream infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Mr. Johnson. You’ve been afebrile all night—great news. Blood cultures are negative at 48 hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Does that mean I can stop antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll stop cefepime and metronidazole today. The fever was likely non-infectious—maybe related to your cancer or chemo.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be tumor-related fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Some cancer patients get fevers without infection. Given your history, that’s a real possibility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I felt fine one day, then sick overnight—no gradual build-up like an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll discharge you tomorrow if you stay well. You’ll follow up with your oncologist for your next chemo cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another ERCP or scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Your imaging was stable, and no signs of obstruction. Your oncologist will decide if and when you need more procedures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’ve had no fever, labs are stable, and cultures remain negative. We’re clearing you for discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So no infection after all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No evidence of it. We think this was a non-infectious fever, possibly related to your cancer or treatment. You’ll go home off antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home medications are continued—atenolol, pantoprazole, terazosin, the nasal spray, and olanzapine for sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, Doctor. I appreciate the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Call your oncologist if you develop fever again or feel unwell. Otherwise, keep up with your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’ll see you only if needed.
